**Answer: Yes, a non-constant function can have a dense set of periods.**

**Proof.**

Recall that $T \neq 0$ is a *period* of $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ if $f(x+T)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. The set of periods $P(f)$ is an additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$, and it is a classical fact that every additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ is either dense or cyclic ($a\mathbb{Z}$). We exhibit a non-constant function whose period group is dense.

**Example (Dirichlet function).** Define
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \in \mathbb{Q},\\ 0 & \text{if } x \notin \mathbb{Q}. \end{cases}$$

*Non-constant:* $f(0)=1$ and $f(\sqrt{2})=0$, so $f$ is non-constant.

*Every rational is a period:* Let $q\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$. For any $x\in\mathbb{R}$:
- If $x\in\mathbb{Q}$, then $x+q\in\mathbb{Q}$, so $f(x+q)=1=f(x)$.
- If $x\notin\mathbb{Q}$, then $x+q\notin\mathbb{Q}$, so $f(x+q)=0=f(x)$.

Hence $\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq P(f)$, and since $P(f)$ is a subgroup, $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq P(f)$.

*No irrational is a period:* If $T\notin\mathbb{Q}$, then $f(0+T)=f(T)=0\neq 1=f(0)$, so $T\notin P(f)$.

Therefore $P(f)=\mathbb{Q}$, which is dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

**Remark (the role of regularity).** If one additionally requires $f$ to be continuous (or even measurable), then a dense period set forces $f$ to be constant: density of $P(f)$ gives a sequence $T_n\to 0$ with $T_n\in P(f)$, and continuity yields $f(x)=\lim_n f(x+T_n)=f(x)$ for all $x$ while also $f(x)=f(x+T)$ for all $T\in P(f)$, so $f$ is constant on a dense set and hence everywhere. Thus the phenomenon is genuinely a feature of *irregular* (discontinuous) functions. $\blacksquare$
